# Jarā Sutta (Snp 4.6 (PTS Snp 158))

**ID:** Snp 4.6 (PTS Snp 158)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Jarā Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Jarā Sutta* ("Old Age") is the sixth discourse of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* in the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 4.6), consisting of ten verses [Pande 1974; Hazra 1994]. The discourse reflects on the brief nature of human life, observing that a person dies even before reaching a hundred years, or eventually perishes from old age [Burlingame 1921]. Its primary doctrinal instruction warns that grief, sorrow, and avarice arise from possessiveness and selfishness; true liberation is found when a person abandons any sense of "mine" and, living an independent, homeless mendicant life, does not rely on another for purification [Arnold and Bowden; Hazra 1994].

Scholars have noted that the *Jarā Sutta* contains verses in the *vetālīya* metre [Ruegg and Schmithausen 1990]. Based on its metrical characteristics and internal structure, scholars such as Tilmann Vetter have grouped it with discourses like the *Kāma Sutta* and *Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta* as appearing relatively later than other portions of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* [Vetter 1988; Ruegg and Schmithausen 1990]. Govind Chandra Pande likewise observes that the ten verses of the *Jarāsutta* display hardly any marked archaic linguistic forms [Pande 1974]. In the commentarial literature, the recitation of this sutta is associated with the conversion of an elderly brahmin couple, who were established in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) after hearing it [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877].

 The text is also cited in the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 1) and received a dedicated canonical commentary in the *Cullaniddesa*/*Mahāniddesa* (*Jarāsuttaniddesa*, Mnd 6). DharmaNexus aligns the sutta extensively with Mnd 6, detecting 40 matching passages (3,451 shared characters), with the longest segment matching §5.1–6.4 to §61.1–62.4 with 0.98 similarity [DharmaNexus].
